hero.title: Daily Journal Template
hero.lead:
A template is the cheapest fix for the blank page. Instead of deciding what to write, you fill in fields — and an entry that takes ninety seconds is an entry that still happens on the night you nearly skipped it.

Below are five layouts, all short enough to be usable and all copyable straight into a notebook, a note, or a journal app. Take one, use it for two weeks, and change the lines that don't earn their place. A template you edited is always better than a template you inherited.

sections.heading: What makes a template work
sections.html:
Most journal templates you'll find online fail the same way: they're beautiful, they have eleven fields, and they get used four times. Three rules keep a template alive.

  • Four to six fields, maximum. Every field is a small tax you pay nightly. Anything you skip twice in a row should be deleted, not felt guilty about.
  • Every field is a question, not a topic. "Reflection" produces a stare; "what went better than I expected?" produces a sentence. Specific questions do the work.
  • Include one open field. Fully structured entries turn into form-filling, and the good stuff — the thing you didn't plan to write — needs somewhere to go.

Also decide, once, what the template is for. A memory log, a stress valve, and a planning tool look different on the page, and trying to be all three is how you end up with eleven fields. If you haven't picked yet, how to start journaling walks through the choice.

sections.heading: Template 1 — the five-minute daily
sections.html:
The default. Balanced between recording the day and reflecting on it, and short enough to survive a bad night. Copy the left column as your headings; the right column is what goes under each one.

FieldWhat to writeTime
Date & moodToday's date and one or two words for how the day felt10 sec
What happenedThree sentences, facts only, no interpretation1 min
How I felt about itThe feeling, named as precisely as you can manage1 min
One good thingSomething specific that went right, however small30 sec
On my mindOpen field — anything still circling2 min

Filled in, it looks like this:

"Tue 12 Aug — flat but okay. Finished the handover doc, long call with Sam, walked back the long way. Relieved about the doc and a bit deflated that nobody noticed it was done. One good thing: the walk. On my mind: whether "nobody noticed" is a work problem or a me problem — I think I want it acknowledged more than I want to admit."

Ninety seconds, and the last line is the one worth having.

sections.heading: Template 2 — the evening reflection
sections.html:
For closing the day rather than recording it. This is the one to use if you journal to sleep better: it deliberately ends by putting tomorrow's worries somewhere other than your head.

  1. Today in one sentence. Not a summary — the sentence you'd say if someone asked.
  2. What went better than expected? Trains attention away from the day's single worst moment.
  3. What drained me? Name it plainly. Over a month, this field becomes the most informative one in the template.
  4. What am I still carrying? Everything unfinished, dumped out.
  5. Does it need to come to bed with me? For each item: park it, or write the next physical action and when you'll do it.
  6. One thing I'm glad about today. Specific. "My family" doesn't count; "the way Dad laughed at his own joke" does.

Steps four and five are the working parts. An open loop keeps you awake because it has nowhere else to be stored — writing down the next action closes it well enough for sleep. If gratitude is the field you keep coming back to, keeping a gratitude journal covers how to keep it from going stale.

sections.heading: Template 3 — the weekly review
sections.html:
Run this once a week, on the same day, for ten to fifteen minutes. It's the highest-value template here by a distance — daily entries record, the weekly review is where you actually read your own life. Skip everything else before you skip this.

SectionPrompt
RereadRead this week's entries first. Don't write anything yet.
PatternWhat came up more than once? What was I circling?
WinsThree things that went right, including the ones nobody would congratulate me for.
DrainsWhere did my energy actually go? Was that the plan?
UnfinishedWhat's still open? What's just going to stay open, honestly?
Next weekOne thing to do more of, one to do less of, one specific commitment with a day attached.

The first row is the one people skip, and it's the reason the review works at all. Rereading a week of your own entries is where patterns appear that no single entry contains — and it turns journaling from a chore into something that visibly pays you back, which is exactly what a durable journaling habit needs.

sections.heading: Templates 4 and 5 — the one-line log and the hard day
sections.html:
The one-line log

For busy stretches, travel weeks, or any period where a real entry isn't going to happen. Format: date — one sentence. That's the whole template.

  • 12 Aug — First day back, inbox survivable, slept badly.
  • 13 Aug — Sam's news at lunch. Still processing it.
  • 14 Aug — Nothing. Rain all day, finished the book.

It looks trivial and it isn't. A year of one-liners is a genuinely useful record, it keeps the habit alive through the weeks that would otherwise break it, and it costs fifteen seconds. Any daily template should have this as its official fallback rather than "skip tonight."

The hard day

Not for daily use — for the days when something has actually gone wrong and the usual fields feel beside the point.

  1. What happened, in plain order, with no interpretation at all.
  2. What I'm feeling, named as precisely as I can.
  3. What I'm afraid this means. Then: is that a fact, or a fear?
  4. What's mine to fix and what isn't. Two lists.
  5. What I'd say to a friend describing this exact situation.
  6. What I need right now — sleep, food, a conversation, an apology, a walk.

Step one does more than it looks. Writing events in plain sequence separates what happened from what you concluded about it, and those two are usually tangled. If the same hard thing keeps returning across many entries without changing shape, that's worth reading as a signal — journaling for anxiety and stress covers the line between processing and rumination.

sections.heading: Where to keep your template
sections.html:
A template only works if it's in front of you at writing time. On paper that means copying the headings onto the next page before you start — or a printed card tucked into the notebook. It's slightly tedious and completely workable, and plenty of people prefer the ritual.

The tedium is the one thing an app removes for free. Feeltracker Daily Journal has reusable templates built in: save any layout on this page once, and every new entry opens with the fields already there. Nothing to recopy, and never a blank page.

The rest of it is aimed at the same problem:

  • Reminders at your hour, so the template gets opened at all.
  • Search across every entry — which is what makes a template pay off, since consistent fields turn into something you can look back through. Search "drained" across three months and the pattern is right there.
  • Calendar and year, month and day browsing, so the weekly review takes seconds rather than flipping pages.
  • Rich text and photos, for the entries where a picture belongs next to the words.
  • Widgets on the home screen, and it syncs across iPhone, iPad and Mac.
  • Private by default — iCloud sync with no account and no email address — and export to PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON whenever you want the archive in your own hands.
  • AI insights over your own writing, free tier included, if you'd like a second read on what your entries keep returning to.

Paper, notes app, or this one: the template matters more than the medium. Pick a layout above, use it tonight, and delete the field you skip twice.

items.question: How many fields should a daily journal template have?
items.answer: **Four to six.** Every field is a small nightly tax, and templates with ten fields get abandoned inside a month. Keep at least one open field for whatever you didn't plan to write — that's usually where the useful entries come from.

items.question: Should I use the same template every day?
items.answer: Mostly yes — the point of a template is that you stop deciding. Keep one daily layout, plus a one-line fallback for busy stretches and a separate template for hard days. Review the fields monthly and delete anything you keep skipping.

items.question: Do templates make journaling feel mechanical?
items.answer: They can, if every field is closed. The fix is the open field at the end: structure gets you started, then you follow whatever shows up. If entries still feel like form-filling, swap two fields for a [prompt](/daily-journal/journal-prompts/) that changes weekly.

items.question: Is a weekly review worth the extra time?
items.answer: It's the highest-value item on this page. Daily entries record; the weekly review is where you read them back and see patterns no single entry contains. If you only have time for one thing, **do the review and let some daily entries go**.

items.question: Can I use these templates on paper?
items.answer: Yes — every layout here was written to be copyable by hand. On paper, write the headings on the next page before bed so the page is ready when you sit down. The only thing paper can't do is recopy the template for you and let you search the fields later.

data.disclaimerText: Journaling is a wellbeing practice, not a treatment. A template can make difficult feelings easier to approach, but writing doesn't replace professional mental-health support. If journaling consistently surfaces distress — persistent low mood, anxiety that doesn't ease, or thoughts of harming yourself — please talk to a doctor or therapist. If you are in crisis, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country.
